questions.q: State the two necessary and sufficient conditions for a thermodynamic process to be reversible.
questions.a: A process is reversible only if (1) it is quasi-static (system remains in thermal and mechanical equilibrium with surroundings at every stage) and (2) it involves no dissipative effects (friction, viscosity, inelastic deformation, unrestrained expansion, etc.). A wrong answer listing only "slow process" or only "no friction" reveals the student misses that both conditions must hold simultaneously – a slow process with friction is irreversible, and a fast frictionless process passes through non-equilibrium states.

questions.q: Why is the free expansion of a gas into vacuum (Joule expansion) irreversible even though no friction is involved?
questions.a: Free expansion is irreversible because the gas passes through non-equilibrium states – pressure and temperature are not uniform during the expansion, so the process cannot be represented by a continuous path on a P-V diagram. A student who says "it is reversible because no friction" confuses the absence of dissipation with the presence of equilibrium; they miss that irreversibility also arises from non-equilibrium intermediate states, which violates the quasi-static condition.

questions.q: An ideal gas undergoes an isothermal expansion from volume V₁ to V₂ at temperature T. The process is carried out quasi-statically but the piston has a small constant friction force f. Calculate the extra work dissipated as heat due to friction if the piston moves a distance Δx, and explain whether the process remains reversible.
questions.a: Extra work dissipated = f·Δx (joules). This energy appears as heat transferred to the gas and surroundings. The process is **irreversible** because friction is a dissipative effect – even if quasi-static, the dissipative work cannot be recovered without leaving a net change in the universe. A student who calculates f·Δx correctly but claims the process is still reversible misunderstands that dissipation, however small, violates the "no dissipative effects" condition for reversibility.

questions.q: Compare the P-V diagrams of a reversible isothermal expansion and an irreversible isothermal expansion (against constant external pressure) between the same initial and final states. Which diagram shows a larger area under the curve? What does this imply about work done?
questions.a: The reversible isothermal expansion shows a larger area under the curve (the curve follows PV = constant). The irreversible expansion against constant P_ext is a horizontal line on the P-V diagram at P = P_ext, giving less area. This implies the reversible process delivers **maximum work** for a given state change. A student who says the irreversible process does more work confuses the constant external pressure with the gas pressure; they fail to see that in irreversible expansion, P_ext < P_gas at each instant, so ∫P_ext dV < ∫P_gas dV.

questions.q: A student argues: "Since the Carnot engine is reversible, its efficiency η = 1 - T₂/T₁ can be exceeded by an irreversible engine that cleverly uses friction to generate extra heat." Evaluate this claim using the Kelvin-Planck statement.
questions.a: The claim is **false**. The Kelvin-Planck statement says no process can have the sole effect of converting heat completely into work. An irreversible engine with friction produces *less* work output for the same heat input because part of the work is dissipated as heat. Carnot's theorem proves no engine (reversible or irreversible) operating between T₁ and T₂ can exceed η_Carnot. A student who agrees with the claim misunderstands that friction *reduces* useful work output, and that reversibility represents the theoretical upper limit, not a lower bound.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment to test whether the condensation of steam on a cold mirror is reversible or irreversible. Specify the system, surroundings, and the criterion you would use to decide.
questions.a: (1) System — the steam and the mirror; surroundings — the room air at room temperature, (2) Criterion — the process is reversible only if it is quasi-static, with an infinitesimal temperature difference at the interface, and free of dissipation, (3) Observation — condensation runs at a finite temperature difference across the steam-mirror interface and releases latent heat into a temperature gradient, violating the quasi-static condition, (4) Reversal test — evaporating the water back needs a hotter source, which changes the surroundings and leaves a net change, so the process is irreversible. A poor answer claiming it is reversible because you can boil the water again misses that boiling requires a hotter source and alters the surroundings.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A ______ process is reversible if it can be reversed such that both the system and the surroundings return to their original states with no net change anywhere else in the universe; it is irreversible if it cannot be reversed without leaving a net change in the universe.
